414.title: Fuel in hand
414.hook: Angiras sends the seeker to a guru with firewood in hand, and that's why students still bring an offering
414.carry: come to the guru with fuel in hand
414.howItsDone: In many Hindu traditions students approach a teacher with an offering and study in the guru-shishya relationship; Guru Purnima, on the full moon of Ashadha, is a day many set aside to honor their teachers.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: plava, the rites as unsteady boats. Good for the lake, not for the ocean. Your line was rites earn a heaven that ends; moksha isn't earned.
screen: `RITES EARN A HEAVEN THAT ENDS; MOKSHA ISN'T EARNED.`

segments.voice: When you show up at someone's house for the first time, you bring something. Because it says: I came on purpose, and I'm not just here to take. The Mundaka itself opens with a visit like that. Shaunaka, a great householder, comes to the sage Angiras the proper way and asks one question: what is it that, once known, makes everything known? Angiras's whole answer is this Upanishad. And right after saying the rites can't carry you across, he says what can: a person, and a bundle of sticks.
screen: `SHAUNAKA COMES TO ANGIRAS.` → `WHAT, ONCE KNOWN, MAKES EVERYTHING KNOWN?` → `WHAT CAN CARRY YOU ACROSS?`

segments.voice: Here's Angiras's verse, Mundaka 1.2.12. Having looked closely at the worlds won by works, a seeker should come to dispassion. The uncreated isn't won by the made. To know that, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher who is learned in the Veda and established in Brahman. Samitpanih: samit, firewood, the sticks for the sacred fire; pani, hand. Fuel in hand. You met this a few days ago, when the six students came to Pippalada samitpanayah, with fuel in their hands. It's the old sign of a real student: I'll serve, I'll help keep your fire going. And notice the two qualities named for the teacher. Shrotriya: learned in the Veda, someone who has heard and studied. And brahmanishtha: established in Brahman, someone who lives what they know. Both. Then the next verse gives the teacher a duty too. To a student who has come properly, whose mind is calm and settled, the wise teacher should teach, truly, the knowledge by which one knows the imperishable. So the student brings fuel. The teacher brings fire. Both owe something. This is one of Hinduism's oldest teachings: guru and shishya, teacher and student. The deepest knowing passes from a person who lives it, voice to ear. It's why students of music and dance still touch a teacher's feet before a lesson, and why Guru Purnima, a full-moon day, is set aside to honor teachers. The offering isn't a fee. It says: I'm here to serve, and to learn.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered: a parent, a coach, an elder. Then ask what fuel you could bring someone teaching you now: patience, attention, showing up.

415.title: Sparks from one fire
415.hook: Angiras shows Shaunaka a blazing fire: every being is a spark of the one fire, and goes back to it
415.carry: every being is a spark of the one fire
415.tomorrow: the bow, the arrow, the target
415.howItsDone: In Hindu homes and temples a lamp or flame is waved before the deity in arati, and some teachers use the sparks of Mundaka 2.1.1 to explain how each being shares in the divine.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: come to the guru with fuel in hand. Today, the fire that fuel was for.
screen: `COME TO THE GURU WITH FUEL IN HAND.`

segments.voice: A bonfire on a cold night. Someone drops on another log, and the fire answers with a fountain of sparks, hundreds of them, into the dark. Each one glows for a second, drifts, and fades. Each one is small. And each one, while it lasts, is exactly what the fire is: the same heat, the same light, the same color. Nobody watching says, look, a different thing just left the fire. The student has arrived with fuel. And the Mundaka's second chapter begins by pointing straight at the fire.
screen: `A BONFIRE ON A COLD NIGHT.` → `A FOUNTAIN OF SPARKS.` → `EACH ONE IS THE SAME FIRE.`

segments.voice: Angiras goes on, and his second chapter opens: this is the truth. As from a blazing fire sparks of the same form fly out by the thousands, so from the imperishable, dear one, beings of every kind are born, and to it they go back. Three things are packed into that picture. First, there are many: thousands of sparks, every kind of being. You, your neighbor, the sparrow outside. Second, they're sarupa, of the same form. A spark isn't a cheap copy of fire. It's fire, small. Third, they go back. Tatra chaivapiyanti: and there they return. The sparks rise from the fire and go back into it. Then the text describes the source. The person, purusha, is divine and formless, outside and inside. Unborn. Without breath, without mind, pure. From that, breath, mind, the senses, space, wind, light, water and the earth that holds everything are born. Then it draws that person as the whole cosmos, with the sun and moon for eyes and the earth from his feet. The schools of Vedanta read the spark differently. Some hear identity: the spark is the fire. Others hear kinship: the soul shares the nature of God, and stays itself. Both keep the fire, and the way home. And both keep one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the atman, the self in every being, shares the nature of Brahman. That includes the person you find hardest. Before you write anyone off, the spark picture asks: what fire did this one come from?
screen: `THOUSANDS OF SPARKS, ONE FIRE.` · `SARUPA: OF THE SAME FORM.` · `AND THERE THEY RETURN.` · `ATMAN SHARES THE NATURE OF BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `VISPHULINGA.`

segments.voice: Fold your hands at your chest, the way many Hindus greet each other, and feel the warmth of your own palms: your spark, small, bright, real. Then picture someone you'll see today, someone easy, then someone hard, and bow to each in your mind: many sparks, one fire. If folded hands aren't your way, just hold each face for one breath.

416.title: Om is the bow
416.hook: Angiras turns meditation into archery: om the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target
416.carry: om the bow, the self the arrow
416.tomorrow: the two birds on one tree
416.howItsDone: Hindus who meditate with om chant it aloud or hold it in the mind, and some teachers use the Mundaka's bow and arrow to describe how the sound gathers attention toward one point.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: visphulinga. Your line was every being is a spark of the one fire.
screen: `EVERY BEING IS A SPARK OF THE ONE FIRE.`

segments.voice: Watch an archer just before the release. The whole body goes still. The breath slows, then stops. The eyes stop darting. For one second there's nothing in the world but the line from the arrowhead to the mark. Let the mind drift to dinner, and the arrow drifts with it. So when the Mundaka wants to describe meditation, it doesn't reach for a cushion or a mountain cave. It hands you a bow.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE THE RELEASE.` → `THINK OF DINNER, AND YOU MISS.` → `THE MUNDAKA HANDS YOU A BOW.`

segments.voice: Angiras does it in two verses. The first: take the great weapon of the Upanishad as your bow. Fit to it an arrow sharpened by meditation. Draw it back with a mind absorbed in that, and hit the target, dear one: the imperishable. Then the second verse spells out the picture. Pranavo dhanuh: om is the bow. Sharo hy atma: the self is the arrow. Brahma tal lakshyam uchyate: Brahman is called the target. Then two instructions. It must be struck by one who isn't careless, apramatta, undistracted. And then: sharavat tanmayo bhavet. Like the arrow, become one with it. When an arrow hits its mark, it doesn't stay separate, hovering an inch away. It goes in. It becomes part of the target. Tanmaya means made of that, full of that, absorbed in it. You met that -maya, made of, a few weeks ago in the Taittiriya: the self made of food, of breath, of mind. Now the text asks you to become tan-maya, made of that. Why is om the bow? Teachers explain that the sound, chanted or held in the mind, gathers attention and sends it. It's one reason so many Hindu prayers, pujas and classes begin with om. And when the mind wanders mid-chant, many teachers say: no blame, just draw the bow again. The next verse adds: know the one self alone, in which sky and earth and mind are woven. This is the bridge to the deathless. And then a blessing: may you cross safely to the far shore, beyond darkness.
screen: `THE UPANISHAD IS THE BOW.` · `OM THE BOW, THE SELF THE ARROW.` · `BRAHMAN THE TARGET.` · `LIKE THE ARROW, BECOME ONE WITH IT.` · then, large: `TANMAYA.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, like a drawn bow, and let a soft om come out on the breath, or simply hear it inside, gathering your attention the way a bow gathers its pull. Let the attention fly to one point, the stillness after the sound. When the mind wanders, and it will, notice it without blame, and draw the bow again.

417.title: Two birds on one tree
417.hook: two birds share one tree: one eats and grieves, one watches, and seeing it ends the grief
417.carry: the one who watches is on your branch
417.howItsDone: The two-birds verse is chanted in Vedic recitation, and Advaita, Dvaita and Vishishtadvaita teachers each explain the relation between the two birds in their own way.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bow. Your line was om the bow, the self the arrow.

segments.voice: Late at night: the third episode, the fourth cookie, the same feed scrolled twice. And sometimes, for a second, another part seems to sit a little above it all, noticing. Huh. Look at me. That part doesn't scold, exactly. It just sees. The Mundaka's third chapter opens with a picture of exactly that. It's older than the Upanishad itself. A tree, and two birds sitting in it.
screen: `THE THIRD EPISODE. THE FOURTH COOKIE.` → `A PART OF YOU, NOTICING.` → `A TREE, AND TWO BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Angiras opens his last chapter with this verse. Dva suparna sayuja sakhaya. Two birds, close companions, always together, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit. The other, not eating, looks on. Commentators read the tree as the body, and the life lived in it. The bird that eats is the self as we usually know it, tasting every fruit, sweet and bitter, pleasure and pain, hungry for the next. The bird that watches doesn't eat at all. It isn't hungry. It just shines there, looking on. Then the next verse tells the story. On that same tree, the eating bird sinks down, confused, and grieves, feeling helpless. But when it sees the other, the Lord, content, and sees that one's greatness, its grief is gone. The eating bird doesn't have to fly to another tree. The watcher was on the same branch the whole time. The verse is older than the Mundaka: it comes from a Rig Veda hymn of riddles. Here the schools of Vedanta part ways, honestly. Advaita teachers read the two birds as one self seen two ways: the watcher is who the eater really is. Madhva's Dvaita school reads them as forever two, the soul and God, close companions who never merge. Ramanuja's school reads them as two, inseparably joined, the soul as part of God's body, with God as its inner self. All of them keep the comfort of the verse, and one of Hinduism's warmest teachings: God isn't far off. The Gita says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. On your worst night, the eater isn't alone on the branch.

418.title: Truth alone wins
418.hook: India's motto comes from the Mundaka, and the full verse makes truth a road, not just a rule
418.carry: truth alone wins, and truth is the road
418.tomorrow: not by eye, not by speech
418.howItsDone: Satyameva jayate is printed beneath India's national emblem on currency and official documents, and Hindu teachers and families quote it as a reminder that truthfulness is part of dharma.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: suparna, two birds on one tree. Your line was the one who watches is on your branch is on your branch.

segments.voice: If you've ever held Indian money, you've held this lesson. Look at the national emblem: the lions, back to back, taken from a pillar of the emperor Ashoka. Underneath them, in Devanagari script, three words. Satyameva jayate. Truth alone prevails. They're on Indian money, on government seals and documents. And they come from the Mundaka Upanishad, the chapter we're reading now. The full verse says a good deal more than the emblem has room for.
screen: `THE LIONS OF ASHOKA'S PILLAR.` → `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.` → `FROM THE MUNDAKA UPANISHAD.`

segments.voice: Here's Angiras's line: satyam eva jayate, nanritam. Truth alone wins, not untruth. Satya, truth, comes from sat, what is, what's real. So truth here is more than accurate words. It's being in line with what actually is. Eva means only, alone. And nanritam, not anritam: anrita is the crooked, the false, the opposite of rita, the right order of things. So: what is real wins. What's crooked doesn't. Then the verse keeps going, and this is the part the coins leave off. By truth the road is laid out, the path of the gods, on which the sages travel, their desires fulfilled, to the place where truth's highest treasure is. So truth isn't only the winner of an argument. It's a road. You walk on it, and it takes you somewhere. That fits the neighboring verses. Just before this, the Mundaka says the self is reached by truth, by austerity, by right knowledge, by the steady life of a student. Truthfulness isn't a rule stuck on the outside of spiritual life. It's the pavement. That's why Hindu teaching counts satya as part of dharma for everyone, and the Yoga Sutra lists it among the first restraints, the yamas, right after not harming. The words became the motto beneath the national emblem when India became a republic, in 1950. It doesn't claim that truth wins quickly, or every day, or in every courtroom. The Upanishad's claim is longer and quieter: over the whole road, what is real holds, and what's crooked doesn't. Which means the small fib counts too. Not as a crime: as one crooked stone in your own road.

segments.voice: Scoop up a glass of river water after a storm. It's brown and swirling; you can't see a thing through it. Set it on the counter and leave it alone. Don't filter it, don't stir it. An hour later the mud has settled, and you can see straight through to the other side. Nothing was added. Something just stopped moving. The Mundaka has spent two chapters on the self. Now it says how the self is seen, and first, how it isn't.
screen: `A GLASS OF MUDDY RIVER WATER.` → `LEAVE IT ALONE.` → `AN HOUR LATER, CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Angiras's verse starts with a list of no. Na chakshusha grihyate: it isn't grasped by the eye. Not by speech, not by the other senses, not by austerity, not by works. That's a surprise, because this Upanishad honored austerity and ritual earlier: the rites were called true, and Brahman itself swelled by tapas. But they're not the hand that grasps it. Then comes the yes. Jnana-prasadena vishuddha-sattvah. By the clearness of knowledge, the one whose being is purified, meditating, sees it, the one without parts. Prasada means clearness, calm, settling, like water once the mud has sunk. It can also mean grace and favor, and the same word names the blessed food given out at temples. Here it's knowledge gone clear. Vishuddha-sattva is a being made thoroughly clean. The next verse says how. The self is subtle, known by thought, by a mind in which the five breaths have entered, and the whole mind of creatures is woven through with the senses. When that mind is purified, the self shines out. So the senses, speech, discipline and ritual aren't thrown away. They're more like the stirring stick and the filter: useful. But the seeing happens when the water stops moving. And the verse ends with meditating: a mind sitting still long enough to become clear. Later Vedanta teachers gave this a name, chitta-shuddhi, purifying the mind, and many explain that this is what japa, worship, fasting and service are for: not to grab God, but to let the water settle.
screen: `NOT BY EYE, NOT BY SPEECH.` · `NOT BY AUSTERITY OR WORKS.` · `BY THE CLEARNESS OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `CHITTA-SHUDDHI: THE MIND MADE PURE.` · then, large: `JNANA-PRASADA.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus do japa: repeating a mantra or a name of God, often on a mala of beads. Om namah Shivaya, or Ram, or simply om. Pick one, or if you don't pray, a word like peace, and repeat it softly. Don't force the mind still, and don't stir. Each time it wanders, come back to the word, and let the water settle on its own.
Prasada, clearness, calm, like water once the mud has settled. In the Mundaka, the self isn't grasped by eye, speech, austerity or works, but by this clearness of knowledge, in a mind made pure.

segments.voice: The Ganga starts in the Himalayas, under a glacier. For its whole long run it has a name, a goddess, temples on its banks, cities that live by it. People bathe in it, scatter ashes in it, sing to it. Then it reaches the Bay of Bengal. A few miles out, scoop up a cup of water and try to say which part is the Ganga. You can't. It hasn't been destroyed. It's arrived. The Prashna used this picture ten days ago, for the sixteen parts. Today the Mundaka ends with it, and turns it on the one who knows.
screen: `A RIVER WITH A NAME AND A GODDESS.` → `THEN, THE SEA.` → `NOT DESTROYED. ARRIVED.`

segments.voice: Here's Angiras's last picture for Shaunaka. Yatha nadyah syandamanah samudre astam gacchanti nama-rupe vihaya. As rivers flowing on go home into the sea, leaving name and form behind, so the knower, freed from name and form, goes to the divine person, higher than the high. Nama-rupa, name and form, is the Upanishads' phrase for everything that makes a thing this and not that: the label and the shape. A river is mostly name and form. Water is water. What made it the Ganga was the name, and the banks. Astam gacchanti is what the sun does at evening: it goes home, it sets. The rivers don't vanish. They set into the sea. Then the next verse makes a bold claim. Sa yo ha vai tat paramam brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati. Whoever knows that highest Brahman becomes Brahman itself. That person crosses over grief and wrongdoing and, freed from the knots of the heart, becomes immortal. As with the two birds, the schools read it differently. Advaita teachers take it plainly: the knower is Brahman, and always was; only name and form fell away. Other Vedanta teachers read becomes Brahman as becoming like Brahman, reaching it, sharing its joy, while the soul stays itself. Both keep the sea. Many Hindus call this goal moksha, release: in this picture, not being wiped out, but arriving. Then the Mundaka closes with a bow to its teachers. Namah parama-rishibhyah. Honor to the great seers. Twice.
screen: `RIVERS GO HOME INTO THE SEA.` · `NAMA-RUPA: NAME AND FORM.` · `THE KNOWER OF BRAHMAN BECOMES BRAHMAN.` · `MOKSHA: NOT ERASED, ARRIVED.` · then, large: `NAMA-RUPE VIHAYA.`

segments.voice: Say your name to yourself once, then your roles: a child of someone, a friend, a worker, whatever you are to people. Gently set them beside you like shoes left at a door; you'll pick them up again. For now, rest in what's here without the labels: breathing, aware, simply being, like wide water.
Astam, going home, the way the sun sets. The Mundaka's last picture: as rivers set into the sea, the knower, free of name and form, reaches the highest, and becomes Brahman.
